subject: Environment
sub_topic: Access and Benefit Sharing — Nagoya Protocol

concepts.name: Nagoya Protocol: Legal Status, Adoption, and Entry into Force
key_dimensions: Adopted in 2010 at COP-10 in Nagoya, Japan; entered into force on 12 October 2014 — distinction between adoption and operationalization dates is a UPSC trap
Relationship to its parent treaty: Supplementary Protocol under the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), not a standalone treaty
India's ratification status (ratified in 2012, before entry into force) vs. countries that haven't ratified (e.g., USA not a party to CBD itself)
Distinction from the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety — both under CBD but address entirely different subject matters

concepts.name: The Three-Pillar Structure of CBD and How Nagoya Operationalizes the Third Pillar
key_dimensions: Three objectives of CBD: conservation, sustainable use, and fair & equitable sharing of benefits — Nagoya exclusively addresses the third pillar
Why the third pillar required a separate protocol: lack of binding mechanism in CBD for ABS, leading to biopiracy concerns
Distinction between what CBD mandates in principle vs. what Nagoya mandates as binding obligation
Bonn Guidelines (2002) as the non-binding precursor to Nagoya — understanding why they were considered insufficient

concepts.name: Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS): Core Definition and Scope
key_dimensions: ABS applies to genetic resources AND associated traditional knowledge (TK) — the dual scope is frequently tested
Scope limited to genetic resources within the jurisdiction of Parties (sovereign rights principle); does NOT cover human genetic resources
Distinction between 'access' (obtaining genetic resources) and 'benefit sharing' (monetary and non-monetary returns to provider country/community)
What falls OUTSIDE Nagoya's scope: genetic resources covered by other specialized instruments (e.g., FAO's International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture — ITPGRFA)

concepts.name: Prior Informed Consent (PIC): Mechanism and Obligations
key_dimensions: PIC must be obtained from the competent national authority of the providing country BEFORE accessing genetic resources — sequence matters
PIC for Traditional Knowledge (TK): must be obtained from indigenous and local communities (ILCs), not just the national government — a critical distinction
Countries may waive PIC requirement in domestic legislation (opt-out provision) — UPSC trap on whether PIC is always mandatory
India's implementation: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) grants PIC for access by foreign entities; State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) for Indian entities

concepts.name: Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT): Content and Legal Enforceability
key_dimensions: MAT is the contractual agreement negotiated between provider and user — must be established before access is granted, working in tandem with PIC
MAT must include provisions for both monetary benefits (royalties, upfront payments) and non-monetary benefits (technology transfer, capacity building, joint research)
Nagoya requires Parties to take legislative/administrative measures to ensure MAT is sought and fulfilled — binding on user countries too
Dispute resolution under MAT: Nagoya encourages inclusion of jurisdiction clauses; challenge of enforcing MAT across different legal systems

concepts.name: Monetary vs. Non-Monetary Benefits: The Annex to Nagoya Protocol
key_dimensions: The Nagoya Protocol's Annex provides an indicative list — it is NOT exhaustive or mandatory, a common UPSC trick
Monetary benefits: milestone payments, royalties, research funding, joint ventures
Non-monetary benefits: sharing of research results, technology transfer, capacity building, joint scientific publications, training — often more valuable for developing countries
India's ABS guidelines specify benefit-sharing percentages — linking Nagoya obligations to domestic implementation

concepts.name: The ABS Clearing-House Mechanism (ABSCH)
key_dimensions: ABSCH is the online platform under Nagoya for sharing information on national ABS legislation, PIC decisions, and MAT — managed by the CBD Secretariat
Publication of Internationally Recognized Certificate of Compliance (IRCC) on ABSCH is the primary compliance verification tool
Distinction between ABSCH and the CBD's main Clearing-House Mechanism (CHM) — two separate but related platforms
Role in monitoring: how user countries use ABSCH to verify that their researchers/companies obtained valid PIC before utilization

concepts.name: Internationally Recognized Certificate of Compliance (IRCC)
key_dimensions: IRCC is issued when a competent national authority grants PIC and publishes access information on ABSCH — it is the 'passport' for genetic resources
IRCC enables tracking of genetic resources from access to utilization — critical for preventing biopiracy downstream
A permit/consent document issued nationally becomes IRCC only upon publication on ABSCH — the national-to-international transition step
Limitations: IRCC tracks access point, not downstream utilization in supply chains — a recognized gap in the protocol

concepts.name: Traditional Knowledge (TK) Protection under Nagoya: Special Provisions
key_dimensions: Nagoya Article 7: Specific provisions for TK associated with genetic resources held by ILCs — separate from general genetic resource provisions
Domestic obligations: Parties must take measures to ensure PIC/approval of ILCs and ensure MAT with ILCs, even when state is the primary authority over genetic resources
Concept of 'community protocols': ILCs can develop their own protocols for engaging with external researchers — Nagoya encourages but doesn't mandate this
India's People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs) as a documentation tool for TK — link between PBRs and Nagoya compliance; also relationship with Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL)

concepts.name: Transboundary Genetic Resources and Shared Resources: Article 11
key_dimensions: When same genetic resource occurs in multiple countries, Parties are encouraged to cooperate to implement ABS — 'encouraged' not 'required' is a key distinction
Challenge: determining which country's PIC is required when a resource is found across borders (e.g., a migratory species or a plant species spanning multiple countries)
Special provisions for genetic resources in areas beyond national jurisdiction (ABNJ) — Nagoya largely silent, creating a gap addressed later by the High Seas Treaty (BBNJ Agreement)
Nagoya vs. BBNJ Agreement: how the emerging High Seas Treaty fills the ABNJ gap that Nagoya does not cover

concepts.name: Specialized International ABS Instruments and Their Relationship with Nagoya
key_dimensions: Nagoya Article 4: Relationship with other international agreements — Nagoya does NOT override specialized instruments but should be mutually supportive

ITPGRFA (International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture): governs 64 specific food and forage crops under a multilateral system — these are EXEMPT from Nagoya's bilateral ABS requirements
WHO's Pandemic Influenza Preparedness (PIP) Framework: governs influenza virus sharing — operates parallel to Nagoya
UPSC trap: Which crops/resources fall under ITPGRFA vs. Nagoya — e.g., rice and wheat are under ITPGRFA; sugarcane is NOT, so falls under Nagoya

concepts.name: User-Side Compliance Obligations under Nagoya
key_dimensions: Nagoya creates obligations on BOTH provider countries (grant access) and USER countries (ensure their nationals comply) — asymmetric compliance challenge
User countries must take measures to ensure genetic resources were accessed legally — 'due diligence' obligation
Checkpoints: Nagoya requires user countries to designate checkpoints (e.g., patent offices, research funding agencies, publication review) to monitor utilization
EU ABS Regulation (511/2014) as a model: how the EU implemented user-side due diligence obligations — relevant for India's export-import context

concepts.name: India's Biological Diversity Act (2002) and Its Alignment with Nagoya
key_dimensions: BDA 2002 predates Nagoya (2010) but its ABS framework was considered Nagoya-compatible — what needed amendment vs. what was already compliant

Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023: key changes — exemption of AYUSH practitioners from ABS requirements, codified cultivated varieties, and relaxed rules for researchers; controversy around weakening ABS protections
Three-tier structure: NBA (national level), SBBs (state level), Biodiversity Management Committees/BMCs (local level) — which tier handles ABS for which type of applicant

Sections 3, 4, and 6 of BDA 2002 as the core ABS provisions: Section 3 (foreign access), Section 4 (transfer of research results), Section 6 (IPR applications) — each triggering different approval requirements

concepts.name: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA): Composition, Powers, and ABS Role
key_dimensions: NBA is a statutory body under BDA 2002, headquartered in Chennai — not a constitutional body, a frequently tested distinction
NBA's role in ABS: approves access requests from foreign nationals/companies and NRIs; negotiates and ensures MAT; can file cases for biopiracy
NBA vs. SBB jurisdiction: foreign entities go to NBA; Indian companies/researchers go to SBBs — the jurisdictional split is a UPSC trap
NBA's power to oppose patents: Section 18(4) of BDA 2002 allows NBA to oppose grant of IPR in India or abroad on biological resources obtained from India without approval — rare but significant power

concepts.name: Biopiracy: Definition, Indian Cases, and Nagoya as a Remedy
key_dimensions: Biopiracy defined: appropriation of genetic resources/TK without PIC or fair benefit sharing, often through patents — Nagoya is the primary international legal remedy
Landmark Indian cases: Neem (EPO patent challenged), Turmeric (USPTO patent revoked), Basmati (RiceTec controversy) — pre-Nagoya cases that motivated India's push for the protocol
TKDL (Traditional Knowledge Digital Library): India's defensive documentation strategy — how it prevents biopiracy by providing prior art to patent offices; distinct from ABS which is proactive
Post-Nagoya: how IRCC and user-country checkpoints theoretically prevent future biopiracy — and why gaps still remain (digital sequence information)

concepts.name: Digital Sequence Information (DSI) on Genetic Resources: The Emerging Frontier
key_dimensions: DSI refers to digital/electronic sequence data derived from genetic resources — whether DSI falls under Nagoya's ABS regime is the most contested current issue
Core tension: once genetic material is sequenced and uploaded to databases (e.g., GenBank), physical access is no longer needed — potentially circumventing Nagoya's PIC/MAT requirements
CBD COP-15 (Kunming-Montreal, 2022): agreed to establish a multilateral benefit-sharing mechanism for DSI — breakthrough decision linking DSI to ABS for the first time
Implication for India: as a mega-diverse country, India stands to benefit significantly from DSI benefit sharing — alignment with India's negotiating position at CBD

concepts.name: Nagoya Protocol and Intellectual Property Rights (IPR): Disclosure Requirements
key_dimensions: Nagoya encourages countries to require disclosure of origin of genetic resources in patent applications — but this is NOT a mandatory obligation under Nagoya itself
India's Patents Act Section 10(4)(ii)(D): requires applicants to disclose source and geographical origin of biological material — India has a stronger domestic requirement than Nagoya mandates
The TRIPS-CBD conflict: TRIPS Agreement (WTO) does not require disclosure of origin; developing countries have pushed for amendment — Nagoya is a parallel track, not a solution to this conflict
WIPO Intergovernmental Committee (IGC): negotiates a treaty on TK, genetic resources, and traditional cultural expressions — complements Nagoya but addresses IPR system directly

concepts.name: Nagoya Protocol Compliance Mechanism: Non-Adversarial vs. Binding
key_dimensions: Nagoya's compliance mechanism (Article 30) is non-adversarial, transparent, and non-punitive — unlike WTO dispute settlement; this is a structural weakness often tested
No international tribunal or binding enforcement body exists under Nagoya — compliance relies on domestic implementation and peer review
COP-MOP (Conference of Parties serving as Meeting of Parties to Nagoya): the governing body — distinct from CBD COP; only Nagoya Parties can vote on Nagoya matters
Contrast with Montreal Protocol's non-compliance procedure: Montreal is considered more effective due to trade measures — Nagoya lacks equivalent economic incentives for compliance

concepts.name: People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs) and Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs): Grassroots ABS Infrastructure
key_dimensions: BMCs are mandated under Section 41 of BDA 2002 at local body level — they maintain PBRs documenting local biological resources and associated TK
PBRs serve dual purpose: documentation for defensive protection against biopiracy AND as a reference for benefit-sharing claims when resources are commercially utilized
Limitation: PBRs are not legally recognized as intellectual property — they establish prior art but don't confer ownership rights to communities
BMC's role in ABS: consulted before NBA/SBB grants access; entitled to receive portion of benefit-sharing amounts — the flow of benefits from NBA to BMC is a poorly implemented aspect

concepts.name: Nagoya Protocol and Agriculture: Tension with Food Security Objectives
key_dimensions: Strict ABS rules can restrict access to crop genetic diversity held in gene banks — tension between Nagoya's benefit-sharing goals and open access needed for crop breeding/food security
CGIAR Centers (e.g., ICRISAT, IRRI): hold massive gene bank collections; operate under ITPGRFA for most crops but Nagoya creates uncertainty for non-Annex I crops in their collections
Farmers' Rights under ITPGRFA vs. community rights under Nagoya: two different frameworks for recognizing farmers' contribution to agrobiodiversity — overlap and confusion in implementation
India's position: pushed for farmers' rights recognition and exemption of traditional seed-saving practices from ABS requirements — partially reflected in 2023 BDA Amendment
